abstract: Active touch provides rich spatial information about object shape. Whether this haptic information can be retained without an explicit memorisation goal remains unclear. Participants explored an unfamiliar two-dimensional raised-dot contour under different sensory conditions and memorisation instructions. Two haptic groups traced the contour hidden from view, either without advance knowledge of the memory tasks (Haptic-Naive) or with explicit memorisation instructions (Haptic-Informed). Reference groups traced the visible contour (Visuo-Haptic-Naive) or viewed it without tracing (Visual-Naive), both without memorisation instructions. Retention was assessed through manual shape reproduction and visual recognition, with a Random-Control group drawing arbitrary shapes as a reproduction baseline. Reproductions in all exploration groups were more similar to the target than arbitrary drawings, supporting incidental spatial encoding in the Haptic-Naive group. Memorisation instructions produced no detectable reproduction advantage but altered exploratory behaviour. Visual feedback improved online tracing without a detectable reproduction advantage over haptic-only exploration. Visual-Naive participants reproduced the shape more accurately than Haptic-Naive participants. Recognition scores were higher following memorisation instructions or exploration with visual information, although Haptic-Naive participants selected alternatives relatively similar to the target. Source-space EEG analyses in the Haptic-Naive group revealed widespread beta-power reductions across bilateral somatosensory, parietal, and occipital regions. Greater reductions in the left lateral occipital complex were associated with more accurate subsequent reproduction. Together, these findings indicate that active touch can support incidental spatial encoding and is associated with changes in cortical activity. The accessibility and use of the retained information are shaped by the goals and sensory context of exploration.
